note.explanation: A chemical bond holds atoms together. In an ionic bond, electrons are transferred and oppositely charged ions attract. In a covalent bond, atoms share electron pairs. In a coordinate covalent bond, one atom supplies both electrons in the shared pair.
examples: Sodium transfers an electron to chlorine: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻; e⁻ + Cl → Cl⁻.
Two oxygen atoms share two electron pairs in O₂, forming a double covalent bond.
note.checkAnswer: An ionic bond forms by complete transfer of electrons; a covalent bond forms by mutual sharing of an electron pair.
note.simple: Ionic means electrons move from one atom to another. Covalent means atoms share electrons. Coordinate covalent means one atom donates the whole shared pair.
note.checkQuestion: What is the main difference between ionic and covalent bonding?
note.title: How atoms bond
steps: For an ionic bond, identify the atom that loses electrons and the atom that gains them.
Write the ions formed and their charges.
State that opposite charges attract and hold the ions together.
For a covalent bond, state how many electron pairs are shared.
For a coordinate covalent bond, identify the donor and acceptor and show the arrow towards the acceptor.
note.answer: Ionic bonding involves electron transfer, while covalent bonding involves mutual sharing of an electron pair.

example.question: Use the formation of sodium chloride to explain how an ionic bond forms.
example.answer: Sodium transfers an electron to chlorine, forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. Their electrostatic attraction forms an ionic bond.

explain.title: What is a chemical bond?
explain.body: A chemical bond is a force of attraction between atoms which holds them together in the form of a molecule or a compound. When the attractive forces dominate the repulsive forces, the system's energy lowers and a stable molecule can form.

explain.title: Ionic bonds: electrons transfer
explain.body: This chemical bond is formed as a result of the tendency of atoms to lose or gain electron or electrons to acquire the electronic configuration of the nearest noble gas because this is a more stable electronic structure. The transferred electrons come from the outermost shells. The resulting oppositely charged ions attract electrostatically.

explain.title: Covalent bonds: electron pairs are shared
explain.body: A covalent bond is therefore a bond formed by the mutual sharing of an electron pair provided by the bonded atoms. One shared pair is a single bond, two pairs make a double bond, and three pairs make a triple bond. The bond symbols are —, =, and ≡.

explain.title: Polar and non-polar covalent bonds
explain.body: Between identical atoms, the shared pair lies midway between the atoms, giving a non-polar bond. Between non-identical atoms, the pair bends towards the more electronegative atom. That atom becomes partially negative and the other becomes partially positive, making a polar covalent bond.

explain.title: Coordinate covalent bonds: one atom supplies the pair
explain.body: Coordinate covalent bond is a type of covalent bond in which the shared electron pair is donated by one atom only. The species which donates the electron pair, is called a donor while that which accepts it is called an acceptor. An arrow head (→) pointing towards the acceptor represents this type of bond. Once formed, it behaves like the other covalent bonds in the species.

mistakes: Do not say that ionic bonding is electron sharing: it forms by complete transfer of electron(s).
Do not forget to write the charges on ions, such as Na⁺ and Cl⁻.
Do not draw the coordinate-bond arrow towards the donor; it points towards the acceptor.
Do not confuse the number of bonds with the number of shared pairs: single, double, and triple bonds have one, two, and three shared pairs.
Do not leave lone pairs out of a dot-and-cross structure when the question asks for the electron structure.
Do not describe a polar covalent bond as electron transfer; the atoms still share electrons, but the shared pair is drawn towards the more electronegative atom.
